analysis.one_liner: Requires gasoline, jet fuel, and heating oil sold in the US to contain growing volumes of coal-derived fuel.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in June 2008 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the President to write rules requiring aviation fuel, motor vehicle fuel, home heating oil, and boiler fuel to include set volumes of fuel made from American coal, rising from 750 million gallons in 2015 to 6 billion gallons in 2022, and at least that share of all fuel sold every year after. Fuel made from coal would qualify if processed at a US plant that captures up to 100 percent of the carbon dioxide the plant releases, and the rules had to ensure the fuel's total greenhouse gas impact was no worse than gasoline. Refineries processing 75,000 barrels a day or less were exempt until 2018 and could seek hardship extensions, and states could petition for waivers.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal producers and any company building coal-to-liquids plants would gain a federally guaranteed market of up to 6 billion gallons a year, backed by civil penalties of up to $25,000 a day for anyone who fails to comply. Refiners, blenders, and importers would have a compliance system modeled on the existing renewable fuel program, and small refineries would be shielded from costs until 2018 or longer.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a guaranteed, mandated market for coal-derived fuel, rising from 750 million gallons in 2015 to 6 billion gallons in 2022, with a floor of at least that share of all covered fuel sold each year thereafter [S3].

Only fuel processed at a US facility capturing up to 100 percent of the carbon dioxide that would otherwise be released qualifies, and the rules must ensure covered uses of the fuel have lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions no greater than gasoline [S3].
Supporters frame the mandate as energy security: substituting domestically produced coal-derived fuel for petroleum in aviation fuel, motor fuel, and heating oil [S2].

Small refineries (75,000 barrels a day or less) are exempt until 2018, may petition for hardship extensions at any time, and the Energy Secretary must extend exemptions where compliance would cause disproportionate economic hardship [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay through fuel prices: refineries, blenders, and importers must meet a yearly volume obligation or face civil penalties of up to $25,000 per day plus any economic benefit gained, costs normally passed through to buyers of gasoline, jet fuel, and heating oil. Coal-to-liquids fuel has historically been more expensive to produce than petroleum fuel, so a mandate functions as a guaranteed premium market paid for at the pump.

drawbacks.text: Coal-to-liquids production is generally more carbon-intensive than petroleum refining, so the mandate's environmental value depends entirely on carbon capture at production plants actually working at up to 100 percent capture — technology that had not been demonstrated at commercial scale at the time [S3].

A mandated volume of a costlier fuel would raise costs for refineries, blenders, and importers, who face civil penalties up to $25,000 per day for noncompliance and would pass those costs to consumers of gasoline, jet fuel, and heating oil [S3].

The definition of qualifying fuel 'may include any other resource that is extracted, grown, produced, or recovered in the United States,' a broad loophole that could let fuels with no connection to coal count toward the mandate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The argument for the bill was energy security and a low-carbon path for coal, but both depend on unproven assumptions: carbon capture working at full scale and coal-derived fuel reaching price parity with petroleum fuel. The costs were concrete and immediate — a legal obligation to buy a specific volume of a more expensive fuel, enforced by daily penalties, ultimately paid by fuel consumers. There were no findings in the record on how much prices would rise, and the bill received almost no support beyond its sponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Shelley Moore Capito introduced the bill with Rep. John Shimkus on June 3, 2008, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1].
The committee took no further action — no markup, no hearing, no vote — and the bill's only recorded actions are its introduction and referral [S5].
It had 3 cosponsors, all Republicans, in a House controlled by Democrats [S4].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and bills not passed by both chambers die at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and anyone opposed to a coal-fuel mandate came out ahead, since nothing was enacted and no one was required to buy coal-derived fuel. Coal-to-liquids developers lost a chance at a federally guaranteed market, though nothing in the bill's trajectory suggested it was close to passage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fuel consumers; coal-to-liquids developers lost a shot

for.name: Rep. Shelley Moore Capito
for.role: Sponsor (R-WV), representing a major coal-producing state
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a mandated market for coal-derived fuels

for.name: Rep. John Shimkus
for.what_they_did: Joined Capito in introducing the bill

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill; its only recorded action was receiving the referral

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic-controlled Energy and Commerce Committee never acted on the bill, and there is no record of any Democratic support.

industries.note: The bill would have handed the coal industry a federally guaranteed market of up to 6 billion gallons a year, enforced by penalties on anyone who failed to blend the fuel. The industry's gain would have come out of consumers' pockets, since coal-derived fuel costs more to produce than petroleum fuel and the mandate forces it into the supply.

They would bear the legal blending obligation and penalty exposure, but small refineries are exempt until 2018 with hardship extensions, and compliance costs are routinely passed through to fuel buyers. The mandate also mirrors the renewable fuel structure they already operate under.
